title: Overseas Clinical Clerkships at the University of Western Australia
paragraphs: I did clinical clerkships for one month at Sir Charles Gardner Hospital in Perth, Western Australia, and for one month at Karratha Health Campus in Karratha.

When writing this account, I looked back at my study abroad goal from last year, and I had set "to learn about various values and experience a world I do not know." Also, because I had spent a year on an exchange program in Canada as a high school student, I wanted to make clear the difference from that time, in that this exchange was after all a part of my clerkships. As a result, I think it became a very satisfying two months.

In Perth I rotated through geriatrics, which is also my preferred specialty, for four weeks. The geriatrics department has two wards, and the one I rotated through was the GEM (Geriatric Evaluation and Management) Unit, which mainly coordinates medication and rehabilitation before discharge or transfer. Patients who had fallen at home and been taken to the emergency department and patients after surgery in other departments were admitted, and the turnover of patients was also high. As for the clerkship content, I took part in daily rounds and conferences, observed the outpatient clinic, took histories myself from patients assigned by the doctor, presented the cases to the doctor, and had discussions. It was difficult to grasp the condition of elderly patients with many complications, but partly because it was a department that was not so busy, the doctor taught me carefully and gave me feedback every time, so I learned a great deal. When I first went to take a history from a patient I was worried whether I would be understood, but elderly people speak slowly, so it was easy to catch, and I was able to practice English conversation quite a lot in the first month, which I think led to confidence in the clerkships that followed. Also, because interprofessional collaboration is especially important in geriatrics, an interprofessional conference was held twice a week for about two to three hours each time. With four weeks there, I could see various interactions and it was interesting. I was also taken along to a physiotherapist's outpatient clinic and on home visits, which was fresh. It also stayed with me that I could hear from the doctor in charge, and of course from those of other professions, why they chose geriatrics and what its appeal is.

In Perth I stayed in a hostel, where I also met many people and talked about all sorts of things every day. I think Australians are especially kind even among foreign countries. Thanks to everyone being there when I got home, I never felt lonely from the first day. Looking back now, I feel anew that they were very fulfilling days, with weekdays prioritizing clerkships and study and weekends devoted to sightseeing and play. It was a livable and beautiful city with many places to visit, and I did not tire of it even after a month.

Karratha, the town where I did my clerkship for the latter month, is a lively town where, because mining thrives, there are many young people working away from home despite its being a rural area, and I was able to see a form of community medicine different from what I had imagined. It was a small hospital with about 40 beds, roughly divided into the general ward, emergency department, obstetrics, surgery and outpatient clinic, and I rotated through the general ward and obstetrics for two weeks each. Most of the doctors were part-time staff who came from other cities. There was no MRI, only CT and ultrasound, and severely ill patients that KHC could not handle were sent by plane to hospitals in Perth, and conversely patients that nearby smaller hospitals could not handle were sent there, so it played the role of a regional core hospital.

In Karratha I encountered for the first time patients of the indigenous Aboriginal people. In Australia, the low standard of living of Aboriginal people, alcohol and drug addiction, and genetic constitution are problems nationwide. Their life expectancy is more than ten years shorter than that of other citizens, and the age of eligibility for nursing home admission is set five years lower only for Aboriginal people. Embarrassingly, I had been completely ignorant of such matters until I came to Karratha, so I was shocked when I saw with my own eyes a young man my own age who already had diabetes, hyperlipidemia and renal dysfunction, and a mother in labor in a state of drug dependence. When I actually talked with them, many were friendly, and I felt that they are simply not interested in their own health and have not received appropriate education. While I keenly felt the importance of medical education, I also learned a great deal from the fact that the approach to patients with poor adherence varied from person to person. As part of medical education I was given valuable experiences, such as doing physical therapy with Aboriginal people in a park and removing lice at an elementary school in a neighboring town. Although there are problems, it was impressive that every doctor spoke with respect for the culture and traditions of the Aboriginal people, and I too actually went to see the Aboriginal art in Karratha.

There was no transport and, honestly, some inconvenience in living there, but since I was able to learn deeply about Australia, I am sincerely glad I came to Karratha for community medicine. Being able to see completely different sides of Australia in Perth and in Karratha was interesting.

Although it was only two months, I was able to form deep connections with more people than I had imagined. An environment where I met new people every day, was taught how they think, and exchanged opinions was very stimulating. Because overseas many things do not get across unless you express your intentions yourself, I made sure to tell the other person properly how much I understood and from where I did not. Many Australians have been to Japan and are pro-Japanese, and whenever I was in trouble someone always helped me. I will keep working hard so that I can repay this kindness someday too.

Finally, that I was able to complete this exchange safely is thanks to the professors of the International Collaboration Office, who watched over us from beginning to end and supported us behind the scenes. I give my deep thanks. I also express my sincere gratitude to the other professors of both Nagoya University and the University of Western Australia who made efforts, and to everyone at the Frontier Association.
